Lesson Overview

In the last lesson, you explored the Total Cost and Lifecycle Improvement Plan for your mousetrap car — every dollar spent, every trade-off made, and every opportunity to make your design better over time. Now you're stepping into the final phase of the Creationeering™ framework: Death & Recycling. It might sound dramatic, but it's one of the most important questions an engineer ever asks: What happens when this is done?

For your mousetrap car, that means thinking about what happens after the competition is over. Will parts get reused? Can the materials be recycled? Or will everything end up in a landfill? Thinking through these questions now — while you're still finalizing your design — is what separates a good engineer from a great one. It's also what it looks like to be a responsible steward of the resources God has given us.

Learning Objectives

Students will:

  • Explain the Death & Recycling phase of Creationeering™ as it applies to engineered systems.
  • Identify the factors that contribute to a product's end-of-life and the options available for its materials.
  • Analyze how material choices affect the recyclability and reusability of mousetrap car components.
  • Apply the OCV method to design decisions that consider the end-of-life of your mousetrap car.
  • Connect responsible design and recycling to biblical stewardship of God's creation.

data.html: Ecclesiastes 1:4–7 (ESV): "A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises. The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again."

The Cycle of Creation and Renewal

Notice what Ecclesiastes is describing: cycles. The sun, the wind, the rivers — none of them stop and start from scratch every day. They flow through a continuous loop, each stage feeding into the next. God designed the natural world with built-in patterns of renewal, and those patterns are all around us.

Your mousetrap car design works the same way. Think of it like a river: raw materials flow in, get shaped into components, power the car during competition, and then — what happens next? Where does your river go? A thoughtful engineer plans the whole course, not just the exciting middle stretch. The Death & Recycling phase of Creationeering™ is your chance to design that ending well.

Responsible design doesn't stop when the project is finished. It asks: What legacy do my material choices leave behind? That's stewardship in action — using God's resources wisely, from first cut to final disposal.

data.html:
What Does "Death" Mean for Your Mousetrap Car?

In engineering, a product "dies" when it can no longer do what it was designed to do. For your mousetrap car, that moment might come when the spring loses tension, a wheel cracks, or the axle bends beyond repair. It doesn't mean the materials are worthless — it means that in this form, the car has reached its limit.

Engineers plan for this from the very beginning. When you chose your materials — wood, plastic, metal wire, rubber bands — you were already making decisions that affect what happens at end-of-life. Some of those choices lead to easy recycling. Others lead straight to a landfill. Understanding which is which is a core engineering skill.

Three Paths at End-of-Life

  • Reuse: Parts of your car could be used again as-is. A good axle, an intact wheel, or a still-functional mousetrap mechanism might have a second life in someone else's project.
  • Recycling: Materials like metal wire or certain plastics can be broken down and reformed into new products. This takes energy, but it keeps resources in circulation rather than sending them to a landfill.
  • Disposal: Some materials — especially mixed composites or heavily glued assemblies — are hard to separate and recycle. They often end up as waste. Good upfront design minimizes this outcome.

Applying the OCV Method to End-of-Life Design

You've used the OCV method — Objectives, Constraints, Variables — to make design decisions throughout this project. Now apply it to the end-of-life question.

Objectives

What do you want to happen to your car's materials after competition? A good objective might be: "Maximize the percentage of components that can be reused or recycled." That's measurable, clear, and responsible.

Constraints

You didn't have unlimited options when you built your car. Budget, availability, and structural requirements all shaped what materials you used. Those same constraints apply now. You can't go back in time and swap every part — but you can document what you'd change if you built Version 2.

Variables

Think about which specific parts of your car could have been made from more recyclable materials. The type of adhesive you used, the kind of plastic on your wheels, whether components were bolted or glued — all of these are variables that affect recyclability. Adjusting them in a future iteration is exactly what engineers do.

data.caption: A disassembled mousetrap car with its components sorted into three labeled groups: Reuse, Recycle, and Dispose — showing how end-of-life planning applies to a real student engineering project.

data.html:
Material Choices and Their Consequences

Let's get specific. Here's how some common mousetrap car materials stack up at end-of-life:

  • Wood (balsa, basswood): Biodegradable and compostable. If uncoated and unglued, it returns to the earth naturally. One of the most earth-friendly options.
  • Steel wire / metal axles: Highly recyclable. Metal scrap has real value and can be melted down and reused many times without losing quality.
  • Rubber bands / tires: Difficult to recycle. Most end up in landfills. Specialty rubber recyclers exist, but they're not widely accessible.
  • Plastic wheels (polystyrene, ABS): Varies by type. Some plastics carry recycling codes and can be processed; others cannot. Always check the number on the plastic.
  • Hot glue / epoxy: These adhesives bond materials together in ways that make separation (and therefore recycling) very difficult. Using mechanical fasteners — screws, clips, press fits — instead of glue makes disassembly much easier.

The big lesson here: design for disassembly. If you can easily take your car apart into its individual materials, recycling becomes much more achievable. If everything is fused together, even recyclable materials become trash.

Design for Disassembly: When you plan your next build, ask yourself — "Could I take this apart in five minutes and sort every piece by material?" If the answer is yes, you've designed something that's much easier to recycle. Minimize glue; favor screws, clips, and press-fit connections wherever you can.

Multiscale Thinking: From Car to Atoms

Here's where engineering gets really interesting. When you look at your mousetrap car, you see wheels, axles, and a spring. But zoom in further — way further — and those parts are made of molecules, which are made of atoms. Multiscale modeling is the idea that what happens at the big scale (your car's performance, its wear and tear, how it breaks down) is connected to what's happening at the smallest scales inside the material itself.

Why does this matter for recycling? Because recyclability is a molecular property. A metal wire can be melted and reformed because its atoms are arranged in a way that allows that process. A cross-linked epoxy cannot, because its molecules have formed permanent bonds that can't easily be broken and re-sorted. When engineers choose materials, they're making decisions that go all the way down to the atomic level — even if they don't think about it in those terms every time.

As you evaluate your mousetrap car's end-of-life, you're practicing a version of multiscale thinking: connecting what you see (a cracked wheel) to what it means at a deeper level (polymer chains that have fatigued and broken) and then to what happens next (can those chains be recycled, or not?).

Your Sustainability Activity: Auditing Your Mousetrap Car

Now it's your turn to put all of this into practice. You're going to conduct a simple end-of-life audit of your mousetrap car design. Work through these steps:

  1. List every component of your mousetrap car — wheels, axles, frame, spring mechanism, string, fasteners, everything.
  2. Identify the material each component is made from.
  3. Categorize each material as: Reuse, Recycle, or Dispose — based on what you've learned today.
  4. Calculate your sustainability score: What percentage of your car (by number of components) can be reused or recycled? What percentage will become waste?
  5. Propose one improvement: If you were building Version 2, what is the single most impactful material or fastening change you would make to improve your end-of-life score? Explain your reasoning using the OCV method.

This audit is a real engineering practice. Companies run lifecycle assessments on their products for exactly this purpose — to find where waste happens and design it out in the next generation.

Don't overlook the small stuff. It's easy to focus on big components like wheels and frames, but small parts — adhesives, rubber bands, tiny plastic clips — often have the worst end-of-life outcomes and are the easiest to overlook. Make sure your audit includes every single component, no matter how small.

Stewardship as an Engineering Standard

Throughout this project, you've been learning that engineering is never just about making something that works. It's about making something that works well, for people and for the world around us. The Death & Recycling phase of Creationeering™ is the final proof of that commitment.

God called His creation "very good" — and part of what made it good was its design. Everything in creation fits together, feeds into something else, returns and renews. As engineers who follow that Creator, you're called to build with that same foresight. Not just "Does this car go far?" but "Does this car honor what it's made of?"

That's the mark of a truly thoughtful engineer. And it's what this entire mousetrap car project has been building toward.

data.title: Going Deeper: Real-World Lifecycle Assessment (LCA)
data.html:
Professional engineers use a formal process called a Lifecycle Assessment (LCA) to measure the environmental impact of a product from cradle to grave. An LCA quantifies things like energy consumed, carbon emitted, water used, and waste generated at every stage of a product's life.

Major companies — from car manufacturers to shoe brands — run LCAs on their products to find where the biggest environmental costs occur and how to reduce them. For example, an LCA might reveal that 80% of a product's carbon footprint comes from manufacturing, not disposal. That changes where engineers focus their improvement efforts.

If you're curious, search for "lifecycle assessment examples" and look at how companies like IKEA or Patagonia publish sustainability reports based on this kind of analysis. It's engineering, economics, and stewardship all working together.
